data.title: Walmart stocks up on inflation-weary shoppers ahead of the holidays
data.description: Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy. The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts. “Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday. Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses. Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook. The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation. “In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday. Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout. This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples. Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings. While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations. Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share. Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals.

data.title: What Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO says about AI anxieties
data.description: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. What AI anxieties? The widespread worries about the threat of AI and the fragility of the tech bubble were eclipsed, at least for today, by Anthropic’s record-breaking public debut. data.title: Venture capitalists digest tech world chaos over cocktails and crab cakes
data.description: WASHINGTON — During one of the most chaotic weeks in recent memory for the tech industry, high-powered executives, founders and politicians gathered at a swanky D.C. hotel for a soirée hosted by one of the largest venture capital firms in the world. As champagne flowed and crab cakes were passed, the tech-tuned attendees digested and debated the seismic shifts in industry and politics, from the historic crash of Nvidia’s CEO to wonders about how a Democratically-controlled Congress will affect business.

data.title: Classified NSA network is still down, leaving some staff working from home
data.description: An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency remained down on Thursday, resulting in some employees being ordered to work from home for a third day in a row, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. The network first went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem that occurred when maintenance on the network was underway. Both sources told NBC News the issue has created an inconvenience, but it has not affected the NSA’s work collecting electronic intelligence around the world and overseeing cyber security. There is no sign that the outage was caused by a cyber attack, the sources said. Even though the NSA’s network issue came amid an unusual series of mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days, U.S. officials have said say there is no indication that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack. Non-essential staff at the NSA are being told to check in with their supervisors and find out if they need to come into the agency’s headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland. Otherwise, they are advised to work from home, according to a telephone information line for the workforce and the two sources familiar with the matter. While the NSA does not release the precise number of agency employees, former officials have said the agency employs tens of thousands of people. In 2024, a Maryland state government document put the number of NSA employees at 39,000. The agency has since made some workforce reductions as part of broader cutbacks across the federal government. The outage also affected a work site in Georgia that handles the NSA’s electronic intelligence work in the Middle East, the sources said. In a statement Tuesday, the NSA acknowledged experiencing a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the statement reads. “NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” The NSA, which oversees the nation’s vast electronic surveillance efforts, is considered one of the world’s most sophisticated cyber security and electronic spy agencies. With powerful eavesdropping and code-breaking tools as well as a well-educated workforce, the NSA prides itself as a center of digital expertise. While it is not uncommon for government networks to suffer from brief disruptions or outages, such a high-profile technical problem threatens to tarnish that reputation the agency has built, according to former officials and experts.

data.title: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
data.description: SHENZHEN, China — Back home, President Donald Trump faces low approval ratings and a resurgent Democratic opposition, but for a couple of satisfying days abroad, he got the respect he relishes. When Trump arrived in China on Wednesday, the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, broke precedent and came out to the tarmac to greet him. And before Trump boarded Air Force One to return home, he strode along a red carpet as a military regiment stood at attention. “Everything was unbelievable ... they treated me as well as the person could be treated,” Trump said in a phone interview with NBC News as he flew home. Coming off the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, the White House felt compelled to post an image alerting Americans that Trump is “still your president.” Trump’s Chinese hosts needed no such reminders. They arranged a memorable bit of stagecraft on Thursday, placing Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an oversized, bagel-shaped table, leaving an impression that the leaders of the world’s nuclear and economic powers were deciding humanity’s future. If there was one image to counteract the notion that Trump is a lame duck whose power is seeping away as Democrats regain control of Congress, that might have been it. Elevating Putin as he wages a grinding war with Ukraine is a gamble for Trump. Much of the international community made Putin a pariah following his annexation of Crimea in 2014 and full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Blowback has been coming Trump’s way, after he agreed to trilateral and bilateral meetings with Russia’s leader and worked the Ukraine conflict into those conversations. Previewing the meetings ahead of the visit, a U.S. official had said the war wouldn’t be raised. In the interview with NBC, Trump said that the summit was, “on a scale of zero to 10 … a 12. It was a great summit and very important. Fantastic relationships built and you know the meetings were good, but the final two and the final three were just amazing, amazing meetings.” Though the leaders discussed the Iran war — “they’d like it to end ... and they’re letting Iran know that” — the meeting “was primarily on Ukraine, obviously,” Trump said. Whether the sit-downs will culminate in a peace deal is far from clear. Two of Trump’s special envoys, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and longtime friend Steve Witkoff, were heading to Berlin on Thursday for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in hopes of a breakthrough. Since taking office, Trump has tried without success to end a Russia-Ukraine conflict that he once promised to settle on his first day. In doing so, he has made no secret of his affection for Putin, raising questions about whether he is a fair broker. The two men met separately in Shenzhen before the trilateral meeting with Xi, with Trump calling Putin a “friend.” That triggered a blunt response — in the U.S. and overseas. “I think Putin’s a thug. I think he’s killing babies and people in Ukraine,” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said Thursday. “I think it’s despicable what he’s done.” Ukraine’s top diplomat in the U.S., Denys Sienik, told NBC News in an interview: “I cannot speak for the president of the United States of America, but as a Ukrainian, Putin is not a friend. Putin is a war criminal.” “Russia attacks Ukraine every single day,” added Sienik, the chargé d’affaires at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington. “When this meeting with President Trump happened in China, Russia attacked Ukrainian cities including the capital of Ukraine.” The embassy sent NBC News a photo that, it said, showed a Russian drone being shot down over the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kyiv on Thursday. The mere act of meeting Putin face to face raises Putin’s stature, signaling to world leaders that the Russian leader should no longer be an outcast. That’s a gift from Trump that Putin hasn’t earned, some foreign policy experts said. “Russia wants to be elevated to the big-boys table and send a message to Ukraine that decisions are being made over Ukraine’s head,” Jake Sullivan, who was White House national security adviser under President Joe Biden, told NBC News. That won’t happen, Trump pledged. Zelenskyy told NBC News this week that any deal that Xi, Trump and Putin negotiate won’t succeed unless Ukraine signs on. Trump has quarreled with Zelenskyy in the past, but on that point, he said they’re aligned. “I agree with him,” Trump said in the phone interview. “I wouldn’t do anything without — he’s the head of that country, so I wouldn’t be doing that.” Putin sounded in no mood for peace at a press conference following his meetings with Trump and Xi. This week, Ukraine repeatedly attacked a bridge that links Crimea and Russia. The bridge is a point of pride for Putin, who sees it as a symbol of Russia’s control of Crimea. Putin said that because of the attacks, Russia would not negotiate and that reprisals would be “painful.” Trump said in the phone interview that the bridge attack came up in his meetings and that Putin was upset over it. But Trump added, “That’s the sad part of war.” “You end up ultimately negotiating,” he said. “I think he [Putin] would like to see it ended.” For Putin to relent, he must face more pressure from abroad, Ukrainian leaders argue. That doesn’t appear to be Trump’s calculation. Last month, he lifted U.S. sanctions aimed at drying up sources of Russia’s outside revenue. As for meeting with Xi, Trump said the two discussed artificial intelligence and American agricultural exports. Hard-and-fast deals, though, seem a ways off. “We spoke about SI [Super Intelligence], and we both agreed that we want— we’re, you know, very much into SI, but we do think that having guardrails, you know, at least on a minimal basis is a positive thing,” Trump said, using his favorite term for artificial intelligence. Asked what he meant by a “minimal basis,” Trump said, “Well, we didn’t get into definitions.” Farmers may see a windfall as a result of the meetings, Trump said. “Because of the relationship, they’re buying a lot of the soybeans and corn and stuff, the agricultural products. I think we’re going to have a great, a very substantial increase in that for the farmers,” he said. Does that mean China committed to buying more agricultural products? “I don’t want to say the word ‘commit,’ but yes, I would, I would say ‘commit.’ … I would view it as something that will move very quickly, and we’ll probably get it done. Let me put it that way,” he said. For Trump, the deference shown to him here and in Manila this week seemed a high point of the trip. In a live interview with Fox News that aired Wednesday evening in the U.S., he was asked what “headline” might come out of his meetings with Xi and Putin. “You saw the greeting yesterday, which in the history of China has never happened,” Trump said of Xi meeting him at the airport, a gesture Trump had extended to Xi in Washington earlier this year. “No president has ever — and this is a highly respected, this is a great president, one of the great presidents of China — and he has never gone to the airport to meet somebody.”

data.title: Tech outages have fueled a blackout panic — and a prepping boom
data.description: The end of the world, apparently, comes with a shopping list. On TikTok and Instagram, people are packing emergency bug-out bags, stockpiling canned goods and showing off big-box store hauls as rumors of an impending nationwide blackout spread online.

data.title: Trump responds to Elon Musk’s ‘I’m not MAGA’ comments
data.description: President Donald Trump warned tech titans against breaking too hard from the conservative movement he’s built up, saying Thursday that he doesn’t think it’ll end well for them.

data.title: ‘Blessing in disguise’: Lobbyists shrug off Stephen Miller’s crackdown on their business
data.description: Just days after becoming White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller tried to send a blunt message to an industry with which he’s long had an icy relationship: lobbyists.
